beats.narration_text: Until now, Gavia only looked at photos. This is Sai. This week it learned to listen: open a recording, and it marks every three seconds where a loon calls. So how does it hear? And how well does it hear through the noise of our own drone?

Click one to hear it, or save every stretch as a spreadsheet. The front page now asks: is that a loon? And it takes almost any recording, even the sound of a video.

beats.narration_text: Under the hood, it's six steps. Decode the file, whatever the format. Mix it down to one channel at forty-eight thousand samples a second. Cut it into three-second windows, back to back. Pass each window through BirdNet two point four, the bird-sound model from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. Out come one thousand twenty-four numbers, and a small classifier turns them into one probability.

beats.narration_text: Each window is three seconds at forty-eight thousand samples a second: a hundred and forty-four thousand numbers. BirdNet turns them into x, the embedding. The classifier scales x, weighs it, and sums it into one score, z. The logistic curve turns z into a probability, and Gavia calls it a loon at one half or more: exactly when z is zero or more.

show.event: the window size typesets
the score z from the embedding
the logistic and its threshold: P ≥ 0.5 ⇔ z ≥ 0

props.title: From one window to one probability
props.conditions: x: BirdNET 2.4's 1,024-number embedding of the window · μ, σ: each number's training mean and scale · w, b: the logistic regression (b = -0.25) · threshold 0.5 · looncall_v1.json; loonet models/looncall/v1

beats.narration_text: On Loon Net's validation set, the classifier scores a perfect one point zero. Don't celebrate yet. Those windows were picked by BirdNet's own score: loon windows above zero point four, the rest below zero point zero two. Easy by construction, and the model card says so. The harder question is the one our field recordings will ask: does a call still register under the drone?

beats.narration_text: So we ran that test again, through Gavia's own Rust code. Clean, it catches all twenty-eight loon windows. At ten decibels of drone noise, twenty-four. At five, nineteen. At zero, where the propeller is as loud as the recording, thirteen. And it never once called a loon among the thirty-seven other windows. Loon Net's own Python agrees to within four millionths.

beats.narration_text: Here's what that looks like in the app. The Maine recording, clean: a loon in four of eight stretches, the strongest call eighty-eight percent. The same recording with the drone mixed in at five decibels: two of eight, the strongest seventy-seven. Both calls are still found, but their quieter halves fall below the line.

beats.narration_text: So: Gavia can listen now, entirely offline, three seconds at a time, with BirdNet's ears and a small classifier. Its perfect score means little. Under our drone at five decibels, it catches about two loon windows in three, and invents none. And it can't yet tell a wail from a tremolo.

props.artifactHeading: Gavia 0.4.0 · Check an audio · one page
artifactLines: Gavia now scores every three-second window of a recording for a loon call, offline.
Inside: BirdNET 2.4's 1,024-number embedding and a logistic regression; a call is P ≥ 0.5, which is z ≥ 0.
Its perfect val score is easy by construction; at 5 dB of drone noise it caught 19 of 28 loon windows, with no false alarms.
BirdNET's licence makes it non-commercial, and it can't yet tell a wail from a tremolo.
